newsitem.title: USA: NYC sees up to $370 mln loss in 1998 from new laws.
newsitem.headline: NYC sees up to $370 mln loss in 1998 from new laws.

text.p: The New York City council on Wednesday estimated that new federal changes affecting food stamps and various benefit programs for legal immigrants could cost the city to lose as much as $370 million in 1998.
The estimate was contained in a report prepared by the council on the fiscal impact of welfare reform on the city.

However, an official with the city council explained that this was a worst-case scenario, explaining that the Clinton Administration has said it would seek to temper some of the changes affecting these programs.
The city estimated that as the law now stands, in 1998 the new restrictions on federal food stamp programs would cause 130,000 legal immigrants to lose their benefits, which total $123 million.
Almost 31,000 legal immigrants who collect supplemental security income would lose their benefits for a total of almost $148 million.
Legal immigranys who collect Medicaid who might lose their benefits total around 18,500. The benefits that would be lost add up to almost $38 million.
About 66,000 citizens who collect food stamps would lose their benefits for a total of about $61 million.

The city council estimated that if welfare caseloads decline three percent annually, the state could reap a windfall of as much as $458 million in 1997 and $515 million in 1998, under the new program that replaces the Aid to Families with Dependent Children program.
New York City accounts for about 66 percent of the state's AFDC caseload.
